extraction.name: MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI
extraction.description: MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Multimodal questions were manually collected by a team of 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials. The collection process involved three stages: selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted, recruiting university students specializing in these majors as annotators to collect questions from major textbooks and online resources, and creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions were collected from major textbooks, online resources, and lecture materials across 30 subjects and 183 subfields. Sources included college exams, quizzes, and textbooks covering Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data quality control involved three steps: (1) using lexical overlap and source URL similarity to identify potential duplicate problems, with suspected duplicates reviewed by authors to eliminate duplications; (2) distributing problems among co-authors for format and typo checking to ensure adherence to a standardized format; (3) categorizing problems into four difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, and hard), with approximately 10% of very easy problems excluded from the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students specializing in the relevant majors were recruited as annotators to collect questions from textbooks and online resources, and create new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoiding data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution. They were advised to select questions without immediately available answers, such as those with answers in separate documents or at the end of textbooks.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects, specializing in the 30 majors covered by the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark aims to push the boundaries of what LMMs can achieve and prove instrumental in developing next-generation multimodal foundation models and monitoring the progress towards Expert AGI. It is designed to measure progress towards Level 3 Expert AGI, which marks a critical milestone denoting an AI system that reaches at least 90th percentile of skilled adults in a broad range of tasks, thus starting to achieve the substitution threshold for machine intelligence in lieu of human labor for many industries, leading to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. The benchmark focuses on college-level subjects which might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark has limitations including potential biases from manual curation, focus on college-level subjects that might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI, and lack of direct mapping between performance on MMMU and 90th percentile of skilled adults. College exams are not the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. The benchmark combines multiple-choice questions with concise open-ended questions to balance complexity and practicality, which may not fully capture all aspects of expert-level performance.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The benchmark is designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It is intended for testing and validation of large multimodal models (LMMs) to measure their expert-level multimodal understanding capability across a broad scope of tasks. The benchmark aims to monitor progress towards Expert AGI and develop next-generation multimodal foundation models.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To further control the quality of our data, we perform two steps of data cleaning. In the first stage, lexical overlap and source URL similarity are employed to identify potential duplicate problems. These suspected duplicates were then reviewed by the authors to identify and eliminate any duplications. The second stage involves distributing the problems among different co-authors for format and typo checking... In the third and final stage, the authors categorize the problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with our design criteria due to their simplistic nature, are excluded from the benchmark.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: In the second stage, we recruit over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to assist in question collection. They collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary. The annotators are instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoiding data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution. Given the arising data contamination concerns of foundation models, the annotators are advised to select questions without immediately available answers, such as those with answers in separate documents or at the end of textbooks.

The few-shot development set includes 5 questions per subject, and the validation set, useful for hyperparameter selection, contains approximately 900 questions, while the test set comprises 10.5K questions... rai:dataLimitations.evidence: MMMU , like any benchmark, has limitations despite its comprehensive nature. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI [57]. However, we argue that strong performance on this benchmark should be a necessary criterion for an Expert AGI system... We shall caution that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI, as per the definition [57], because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and '90th percentile of skilled adults,' nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle... To strike a balance between complexity and practicality, MMMU combines multiple-choice questions with concise open-ended questions, enabling the assessment of diverse subjects while addressing the challenges associated with evaluating open-ended responses.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We introduce MMMU : a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning... MMMU is designed to measure three essential skills in LMMs: perception, knowledge, and reasoning. Our aim is to evaluate how well these models can not only perceive and understand information across different modalities but also apply reasoning with subject-specific knowledge to derive the solution... Our aim with MMMU is to push the boundaries of what LMMs can achieve. We believe it will prove instrumental in developing next-generation multimodal foundation models and monitoring the progress towards Expert AGI.
